data.title: Conditional types
data.subtitle: T extends U ? X : Y, distribution, infer

cards.front: How do you read T extends U ? X : Y?
cards.meaning: At the type level, extends means is assignable to, not class inheritance. The conditional picks X if T is assignable to U, otherwise Y. IsString<'hello'> is true; IsString<42> is false.
cards.example: type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

cards.front: What is ToArray<string | number> when ToArray is T extends any ? T[] : never?
cards.meaning: When T is a naked type parameter and a union, the conditional distributes once per member: string[] | number[], not (string | number)[]. Evaluation is ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>. This is how Exclude and Extract filter unions. Expecting a single array of the union is the usual trap.
cards.example: type Result = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]

cards.front: When does a conditional distribute over a union?
cards.meaning: Only when the checked type is a naked type parameter — just T, not wrapped in a tuple, array, or similar — and T is a union. Distribution runs the conditional once per member, then unions the results.

cards.front: How do you treat a union as one unit in a conditional?
cards.meaning: Wrap the type parameter so it is not naked, e.g. [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never. Then ToArrayNonDist<string | number> is (string | number)[], not string[] | number[].
MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T. Each union member is tested; matches become never and disappear from the union — never members vanish. Do not reinvent it for ordinary union filtering.
MyExtract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never. Members assignable to U are kept; the rest become never and vanish. Complementary to Exclude.

Inside an extends clause, infer Name introduces a new type variable bound to whatever matched that position, usable in the true branch. You cannot use infer outside an extends clause. If the pattern does not match, the false branch runs (often never).
cards.notes: Using infer outside extends is a listed misconception.

cards.meaning: string, and never. ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never infers the array element when T matches an array; otherwise the false branch is never. Flatten one level without never by using T on the false branch: T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T.
cards.example:
type A = ElementType<string[]>; // string
type C = ElementType<string>; // never

cards.front: How do you sketch ReturnType with infer?
cards.meaning: F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never captures the return type R when F is a function type; otherwise never. Prefer the built-in ReturnType rather than reimplementing it poorly.

cards.front: How do you sketch Parameters with infer?
cards.meaning: F extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never binds P to the argument tuple. Function I/O types should use ReturnType and Parameters rather than custom copies.
cards.example: type MyParameters<F> = F extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never;

cards.front: How do you sketch recursive Awaited with infer?
cards.meaning: T extends Promise<infer U> ? MyAwaited<U> : T unwraps nested promises until a non-Promise remains. MyAwaited<Promise<Promise<string>>> is string. Prefer the built-in Awaited to unwrap Promise.

cards.front: What does T extends { id: infer Id } ? Id : never capture?
cards.meaning: If T has an id property, infer binds Id to that property's type and the true branch returns it; otherwise never. Pattern for 'property type if present'.
cards.example: type IdOf<T> = T extends { id: infer Id } ? Id : never;

cards.meaning: Derives the resolved DTO type from the service method so compile-time types track implementation instead of a hand-duplicated interface. A Nest/React sketch with a generic ServiceResult is usually just Awaited<ReturnType<typeof service.method>>.

cards.front: When should you write a custom conditional type?
cards.meaning: Day-to-day app code rarely needs hand-rolled conditionals; use Exclude, Extract, Awaited, ReturnType, Parameters. Write a custom one when deriving from an existing function or API shape would otherwise drift, or when building a shared library util — not for one-off DTOs. Deep recursive conditionals for one-off app DTOs are overkill and can slow the checker.

cards.front: What happens with never extends X ? A : B?
cards.meaning: never distributes, which can surprise you because never is an empty union — distribution over no members yields never. Empty-union distribution is the edge case to name, not a simple 'never is assignable to everything' shortcut.
cards.notes: never extends X is not a simple 'never is assignable to everything' interview shortcut once distribution applies.

cards.front: Does the order of extends checks matter?
cards.meaning: Yes, for overlapping patterns. Put more specific patterns first, like overload order. A later, broader match can steal cases the specific branch should have taken.
